name: Agent sandboxing
description:
We've previously recommended sandboxed execution for coding agents. As AI agents become increasingly autonomous and capable of acting not only in coding environments but also in business systems, restricting their operational scope has become critical. We now consider agent sandboxing a sensible default for all agents. Running agents in isolated environments with restricted privileges and access to external systems reduces the risk and limits the impact of unexpected behavior, unintended actions or malicious exploitation.


We recommend teams apply a risk-based approach to sandboxing, informed by threat modeling of their agents and systems. Although there is no one-size-fits-all solution, recent security headlines reinforce the importance of applying established security practices, such as the principle of least privilege, when building and running agents.
relatedBlips: Threat modeling;Sandboxed execution for coding agents

name: Mutation testing
description:
Mutation testing evaluates test suite quality by automatically introducing small, artificial bugs into application code and verifying that at least one test fails. If tests pass despite the code change, the mutation survives, revealing gaps in test coverage or assertion quality. As teams adopt AI coding assistants, the volume of AI-generated code and tests increases rapidly, making traditional code coverage metrics easier to inflate with superficial tests that lack meaningful validation.


This technique acts as a guardrail, helping ensure generated tests don’t simply pass without catching logic changes.


Beyond dedicated frameworks, AI agents can now perform mutation testing autonomously during execution by directly modifying code, running tests and evaluating assertions in their loop. Because automated mutation runs are time-consuming, developers should target specific internal packages or rely on incremental checks to run tests only on recently changed code.

name: Path-to-production mapping
description: Path-to-production mapping is a standard practice at Thoughtworks that has become newly relevant with the advent of agentic coding. Increased code throughput can expose or amplify bottlenecks elsewhere in the path-to-production, making it essential for teams to optimize the end-to-end flow of software rather than coding speed alone. The activity is most often done in a workshop that includes everyone involved in designing, developing, releasing and operating the software. First, participants list the steps in the process on a whiteboard, from the developer workstation all the way to production. In a second pass, they capture pain points. The activity is often eye-opening, as participants identify delays, risks and inconsistencies they weren’t previously aware of. Tackling those bottlenecks is key to improving overall delivery productivity.

name: Post-quantum cryptography
description:
Post-quantum cryptography (PQC) refers to cryptographic algorithms designed to protect digital data against attacks by future quantum computers. As quantum computing advances, the threat to conventional encryption becomes increasingly real: data encrypted today can be harvested now and decrypted later, making key exchange the most urgent area to migrate. With NIST's standards now finalized (ML-KEM, ML-DSA and SLH-DSA), governments worldwide target migration between 2030 and 2035.


Modern infrastructure, languages (for example, Java since JDK 24) and frameworks are increasingly providing native PQC support in their latest versions. Enabling it, though, requires upgrading from older releases or adjusting configurations. Organizations should mandate quantum-resilient cryptography for greenfield projects while accelerating migration roadmaps for legacy systems.

name: Progressive context disclosure
description:
Progressive context disclosure is a context engineering technique for providing information to LLMs on demand. The system bootstraps the LLM with essential context and allows the LLM's responses or user input to trigger the loading of additional data. We're moving progressive context disclosure to Adopt because the practice is nearly universal in serious applications, although it takes many forms.


In coding, one example is to keep your AGENTS.md lean and provide links to documentation that the agent can look up when needed. Coding harnesses also use this approach to defer the full context cost of MCP tools and agent skills until they're used. Business applications might use vector RAG or GraphRAG to retrieve additional information based on user input. In each case, progressive context disclosure can reduce token consumption and costs and help counter context rot.

name: Threat modeling
description:
Threat modeling is an exercise for identifying potential threats to your systems. It’s a core security practice for all software development, especially for generative AI applications, whose distinctive security risks, such as prompt injection and autonomous action, may be missed by rule-based checks and scans. Threat modeling should be a regular, human-led part of the software development lifecycle, with support from agents. The discussion helps surface undocumented behaviors and build stakeholder understanding.


We recommend starting with known threats and mapping them to your context. Useful resources include the MITRE ATLAS catalog of AI threats, MAESTRO as a companion to frameworks such as STRIDE and toxic flow analysis for reasoning about where prompt injection might enter. A session should end with explicit decisions about where nondeterministic model behavior is acceptable, where it isn’t and where deterministic guardrails are needed to limit risk and harm.
relatedBlips: MITRE ATLAS;Toxic flow analysis for AI

name: Agent plugin marketplace
description: An agent plugin marketplace is a means of distributing harness assets across an organization. The need arises when multiple teams adopt coding agents and want to share skills, instructions, MCP servers, subagent definitions and other assets. Copying these between repos provides no easy way to publish, discover or update them. We've implemented an agent plugin marketplace using documented Git repositories, with plugins in the Agent Plugins format that coding agents consume directly or that are managed as dependencies with Agent Package Manager. Anthropic popularized the pattern with its Claude Code plugin marketplace, and hosted registries such as Tessl's and community collections like wshobson/agents have adopted the idea. We see agent plugin marketplaces as a practical way to make your enterprise harness available across the organization.
relatedBlips: Agent Plugins;Agent Package Manager;Enterprise harness;Claude Code plugin marketplace

name: Agent-maintained knowledge bases
description:
With agent-maintained knowledge bases, a team keeps its shared knowledge in linked plain-text files, often in an Obsidian vault, and uses a coding agent to maintain them. Andrej Karpathy's LLM Wiki describes the pattern: raw sources the agent reads but never changes, a wiki it maintains and a schema that guides how it does it. OpenWiki applies a narrower version of the idea to a single code repository's documentation. The technique is practical today because general-purpose coding agents can already read and edit files effectively, while Git provides version control.


Many people start with a personal "second brain." We recommend taking the next step and sharing one across a team, although expanding it into an organization-wide knowledge base takes more than pointing a coding agent at a folder of files. Generated knowledge can drift from reality, and without regular human effort to keep it accurate, the knowledge base risks creating AI-driven documentation sprawl.


Several of our teams use variations of this approach, with product managers, designers, developers and their agents all querying the same knowledge base. These teams find their information more connected and accessible.

name: Anchoring coding agents to a reference application
description:
Anchoring coding agents to a reference application addresses the challenge of application template decay by separating lean, structural scaffolding templates from evolving platform configuration rules. Previously, we focused on using live, compilable reference applications to keep generated code in sync with current practices. We’re now seeing teams successfully extend this pattern to AI-driven scaffolding.


Traditional code generators and scaffolding CLI tools quickly fall behind as platform guidelines, dependencies and architectural best practices change. Instead of hardcoding these rules into static templates, coding agents query centralized, up-to-date information sources, such as an OpenWiki or structured agent-maintained knowledge bases, at runtime to retrieve current conventions and settings. Consolidating evolving platform rules into unified, agent-accessible repositories helps agents generate code that follows current standards without requiring continuous updates to the underlying scaffolding tools.

name: Coding harness for general-purpose agents
description:
Teams building agents for non-coding work, such as document processing, operations support or migration planning, have typically started with an agent framework and assembled the agent loop themselves. Increasingly, we see teams instead build on a coding harness for general-purpose agents, reusing the runtime of a mature coding agent. Popular coding agents now expose their runtime programmatically through the Claude Agent SDK, the Codex SDK and app-server, OpenCode's server and SDK or Pi's SDK and RPC mode. These harnesses already handle complex aspects of the agent loop, including compacting context on long-running tasks, persisting sessions and running headlessly with the same agent skills, subagents and instructions used in interactive coding-agent sessions. Compared with agent frameworks, the trade-off is less control in exchange for a runtime that's already been tested extensively. We’ve used this approach to build an internal accelerator for .NET application migrations.


However, these harnesses differ in their capabilities. Codex and the Claude Agent SDK provide sandboxing and approval policies, while Pi deliberately leaves guardrails to extensions, making it easier to adapt but requiring more work. Because these runtimes are designed for software development, their system prompts and built-in tools tend to steer agents toward writing and running code. Teams should review these defaults for their intended domain. They should also monitor costs, since coding-agent loops can consume substantial numbers of tokens, and large built-in prompts add to every turn. That's one reason minimal harnesses such as Pi are attractive.

name: Feedback flywheel
description:
In the previous Radar, we described the feedback flywheel as a way to improve a coding agent's harness from earlier sessions. Most developers update AGENTS.md files and agent skills when an agent gets something wrong, but what one developer learns may not be shared with the rest of the team. The feedback flywheel adds a question at the end of each session, asking whether anything should change in a shared artifact, along with a retrospective item where the team decides what to update. Feedback sensors show which checks keep failing, an agent suggestion box collects problems agents report and tools such as Backpass propose edits based on past sessions for a human to accept or reject. We're moving feedback flywheel to Trial because harness edits are now routine.


The flywheel needs to remove as well as add. Rules that only accumulate become agent instruction bloat, and a sensor that produces only noise should go. We recommend continuously checking which artifacts are still used and up to date. Context profiling shows whether edits are increasing what each session loads. Where a self-improving harness has an agent run the loop, the feedback flywheel makes it a team habit, with agents proposing changes and people choosing which changes to make.

name: Graph-grounded codebase reasoning
description:
As context-heavy workflows become more common, sending full source files or unstructured text to LLMs increases token costs. Graph-grounded codebase reasoning addresses this by representing code, documentation and relationships as a structured graph, allowing agents to retrieve relevant subgraphs as context. Tools such as ⁠Graphify capture structural dependencies, helping agents identify relationships that text-based retrieval may miss.


However, graph grounding comes with trade-offs. Recent research suggests agents can sometimes perform worse with graph-based context than with simpler tools such as find and grep. We’ve placed the technique in Trial to encourage readers to explore when graph-based context improves efficiency and accuracy, building on our previous blip on code intelligence as agentic tooling.

name: Grilling
description: Grilling is a technique in which a coding agent interviews you about a plan before acting to resolve potential areas of ambiguity. The best-known example comes from mattpocock/skills, but other skills libraries have their own versions. One benefit is that grilling discourages coding agents from guessing where your intent is unclear. It surfaces assumptions the coding agent might otherwise make on its own. Another advantage is that it helps counter codebase cognitive debt. The grilling process forces you to examine your own assumptions, leaving you with a better understanding of the implementation plan that can be captured in decision records. Our teams have found grilling a useful addition to their agentic coding practice.

name: Interactive visual plans with agents
description: Interactive visual plans with agents are self-contained HTML or MDX plans with diagrams, user flows and wireframes that teams can explore before implementation. Our teams find that stepping through these artifacts makes it easier to verify intent and review complex changes than reading long text plans. Our teams warn against using this technique for "big upfront designs" and favor a more iterative approach, breaking work into smaller, verifiable steps to build understanding along the way. The same approach can provide a visual recap of completed work, but our teams find recaps most useful when the implementation deviates from the original plan. We recommend using interactive visual plans with agents to build shared understanding and establish a human review point before agents implement changes.

name: Managed agents runtime
description:
Managed agents runtime is the practice of running software delivery agents on a platform that manages their execution, infrastructure and operational needs rather than relying on a developer's workstation. The runtime hosts the agent loop and provides sandboxed compute, triggers, credential handling, session state and observability, leaving teams to define the model, prompt, tools and skills. Long-running, asynchronous work is well-suited to background agents that pick up tasks from issues, pipelines or schedules and submit pull requests for review.


Coding tools are converging on this approach, with Cursor cloud agents, the GitHub Copilot coding agent and OpenAI Codex cloud tasks all running in remote sandboxes. Claude Managed Agents offers a general-purpose equivalent. Our internal security team runs a daily agent that triages endpoint detection false positives and proposes rule changes. "Managed" doesn't necessarily mean someone else's cloud. At one client, we run custom agents on a self-hosted runtime in a continuous loop across multiple repositories, fixing code smells flagged by scanners and upgrading dependencies along with any required code changes.


A hosted service is often the easiest place to start, but organizations with data residency, security or integration constraints may need their own platform. Either way, we recommend treating the runtime as production infrastructure, with agent sandboxing and version-controlled agent definitions.

name: Open-weight models
description:
Open-weight models, where model weights, architectures and inference code are publicly released, have reached a significant inflection point. Attracted by their lower total cost of ownership, we’ve been evaluating the latest models from families such as DeepSeek, GLM and Kimi for production delivery work requiring complex reasoning and high-quality code generation, and we’re seeing good results.


Beyond cost efficiency, open-weight models provide deployment flexibility, freedom from vendor lock-in and stronger data sovereignty. Engineering teams can right-size their deployments, from lightweight flash models to hundred-billion- or trillion-parameter mixture of experts (MoE) models, and perform private fine-tuning using domain data. Although self-hosting requires greater operational effort, major cloud providers now offer managed open-weight models that lower the barrier to adoption. Rather than treating them merely as budget options, organizations should evaluate open-weight models for a broad range of enterprise workloads, well beyond coding.

name: Risk-tiered human oversight
description:
Risk-tiered human oversight aligns review depth with what a change could break. Reviewing everything with the same intensity ends in human-in-the-loop theater. We suggest systematically triaging changes. The riskiest or hardest-to-reverse changes are reserved for humans to apply. Intermediate-risk changes go through human review. Low-risk changes can be auto-merged by coding agents through a continuous integration pipeline.


Two strategies can help us decide which changes need more review. Zones in the codebase require elevated review with particular files or directories, while LLM-based change classification analyzes the impact of changes but is fallible. Meta's published process combines these two approaches. Our teams find risk-tiered human oversight an effective way to make the best use of scarce human attention.

name: Self-improving harness
description:
A self-improving harness uses agents to analyze execution traces and evaluation feedback, then propose or implement improvements to the system surrounding the model, including prompts, context strategies, workflows, skills, tools, memory and middleware. The idea isn’t new: techniques such as the feedback flywheel use successes and failures from coding-agent sessions to improve the harness but still rely on humans to interpret the feedback, decide what to change and update the system. Recent research explores a more self-directed approach. Meta-Harness and VERSE use execution traces and evaluation results to improve harness code; VERSE also evolves the optimizer’s own tools and procedures. Lilian Weng’s overview traces this progression from prompt optimization to harness evolution.


Observability and programmability are essential to this transition. Observability helps agents diagnose failures from execution traces and connect changes to measurable outcomes, while programmability gives agents access to components they can inspect, modify and test, expanding the scope for self-improvement. Pi’s extensions, Claude Code Mods and DeepSeek Harness (DSH) illustrate this direction through extensible context, workflows, tools and harness components.


Greater openness creates more opportunities for improvement, but gains still require validation. We recommend bounded experiments with regression testing, while humans define objectives, set modification boundaries and assess whether improvements generalize to new tasks.

name: Small language models
description:
We continue to see a shift in the industry away from a "bigger is better" mindset toward improving artificial intelligence through high-quality training data, model distillation and quantization. Small language models (SLMs) have become increasingly useful for specific tasks that don't require the computational resources of larger models. As organizations face rising costs from running LLMs, teams are recognizing the value of choosing the right model for the task.


Compact models are also viable for edge computing, as Apple Core AI demonstrates by running small foundation models directly on devices.


Our teams have found SLMs effective for narrow, high-frequency tasks that don’t require extensive knowledge or complex reasoning, such as summarization, structured data extraction, intent classification for request routing and basic coding. Unless an agentic use case requires multi-step reasoning or reliable tool calling, teams should consider an SLM as a lower-cost, lower latency alternative.

name: Stateful guardrails
description:
Stateful guardrails extend LLM guardrails from single messages to whole conversations. Instead of checking only the current user message or the final model response, they evaluate a compact transcript of recent turns against policy-specific checks and maintain strike or ban state across the session. This matters because unsafe intent can emerge gradually: each message may look acceptable on its own, while the conversation as a whole reveals attempts at policy evasion, jailbreaking or prompt extraction. In practice, stateful checks run as a runtime gate before the agent acts, working alongside conventional single-turn input and output guardrails.


Evaluating conversation history on every turn adds latency and cost, and strike or ban thresholds need tuning to prevent false positives from locking out legitimate users. Our teams have used this technique in a production conversational assistant for sensitive workflows, tracing guardrail decisions in Langfuse. We recommend that teams running multi-turn assistants in production try stateful guardrails rather than relying on per-message checks alone.

name: Subagents for better context management
description:
Subagents for better context management is the practice of delegating work to subagents to keep it out of the orchestrating agent's context. Exploration, tool output, retries and intermediate reasoning stay in the subagent, and the main session receives a short summary. Most people first use subagents to run tasks in parallel or form a role-based team of coding agents. Protecting the orchestrator's context is another reason to use them. Whatever remains in the orchestrator's context competes for its attention on subsequent turns. Pulling a subagent’s full transcript into the main thread to check its progress undoes this benefit. Useful guidelines include running two to four subagents at a time and keeping tasks that require the same understanding of the code within one agent, so multiple agents don't each have to rebuild that understanding.


Using subagents to protect the orchestrating agent’s context is a form of context engineering that’s easy to try because most coding agents support subagents, and the change is largely in the instructions. We've used cheaper models for subagents handling narrow tasks such as research, potentially reducing costs compared with blanket frontier model usage. We're placing the technique in Trial because its benefit hasn't been measured systematically. The evidence so far comes from practitioners' accounts of their own sessions, without detailed token accounting. We've also observed that the same model with the same prompt uses subagents differently depending on the harness. Teams trying this approach should use context profiling to check whether the orchestrator's context actually shrinks.

name: Toxic flow analysis for AI
description:
As AI agent capabilities expand, teams are increasingly deploying systems that face a lethal trifecta of security risks: access to private data, exposure to untrusted content and the ability to communicate externally. This combination creates opportunities for attacks such as prompt injection and tool poisoning. To address these risks, we've moved toxic flow analysis for AI to Trial.


While general threat modeling provides a broad security foundation, toxic flow analysis focuses on identifying unsafe data paths through agentic systems. These risks aren't limited to standard integrations. They can also arise from malicious agent skills that appear useful but contain hidden instructions to exfiltrate sensitive data. We've successfully used tools such as Agent Scan to perform this analysis, helping teams identify and mitigate unsafe data paths before they're exploited.

name: Unattended overnight agentic builds
description:
Unattended overnight agentic builds refers to the practice of giving a coding agent a feature-sized piece of work when the team leaves for the evening and reviewing what it produced the next morning. We've done this with epic-level features and infrastructure tasks that can take hours. One agent is enough, without a coding agent swarm, although it may use subagents. One Thoughtworks team spends the day collaborating on plans and specifications and leaves the coding to agents overnight. "Overnight" is in the name because it's hard to fake. A team that can do this will likely run similar jobs during the day too. (A team that doesn't leave an agent coding unwatched overnight probably isn't running fully autonomous work during the day either.)


Like microservice prerequisites, this practice has entry requirements, and pushing teams to meet them is a big part of its value. Agents need sandboxed execution, work specified up front as in spec-driven development and feedback sensors so they can correct their own mistakes. A night's work can be too large a batch to review effectively line by line, so teams need a harness they've tested to validate the changes instead of relying on human code review. Complementary techniques include running the agent in a managed agents runtime and letting agents keep the build green by fixing pipeline failures themselves. We've placed this in Trial for teams that have those foundations; for other teams, it's a goal that justifies building them.

name: Agent pipeline responsibility
description:
Agent pipeline responsibility incorporates coding agents into the team's accountability for keeping the build green. An agent that can’t see the build status can’t respect a team agreement not to push on red, while a human relaying failure logs into a chat window becomes a meat proxy.


We recommend making the build state part of the agent’s context. Expose pipeline status and logs through the agent's tools so it can see what went wrong and help fix it. Enforce important rules mechanically with pre-push and server-side gates to prevent agents from pushing broken changes. The increased commit rate from coding agents is leading teams to rethink assumptions around build discipline through techniques such as risk-tiered human oversight. Include the role of agents in your build policy when conducting path-to-production mapping.

name: Agent suggestion box
description:
An agent suggestion box gives a running agent somewhere to report the problems it encounters, such as a bug in a tool or a dependency missing from its environment. When an agent's only output is a pull request or a structured verdict, it may work around the problem without anyone hearing about it. The next session then hits the same problem again. The box can be a Slack channel, a memory store or an issue tracker. Lovable calls its version a "vent tool," and agents-feedback offers one for coding agents. Memory can help an agent avoid a broken tool, but a suggestion box gets the tool fixed. The technique works for business agents in production as well as for coding agents.


We've used an agent suggestion box with an agent that starts a fresh session each day to draft detection engineering rules. A second agent deduplicates the reports. The same report from several sessions is a clear signal, although some reports are subjective or transient. With the box in place, runs went more smoothly, and we had a list of improvements to make. The suggestions still need to be reviewed and acted on, for example, through self-improving harness. We're placing agent suggestion box in Assess because our experience comes from one agent. Lovable merges about ten fixes a day from its vents but reports that roughly half the fixes its triage agent proposes are false positives.

name: Context profiling
description:
As token costs have risen and the industry has left the tokenmaxxing fad behind, developers are looking for ways to manage token usage. The old advice that you should always measure before optimizing still applies. Context profiling means analyzing where your token spend is going (for example, are tokens being spent on file reads or MCP tool calls?). Intuition is a poor guide to identifying which optimizations are worthwhile, especially when you factor in caching, model tiers and promotional pricing. Mature tooling hasn't yet emerged, but you can make do by analyzing your agent sessions or data from tools such as Entire CLI and AgentsView.


In our experience, the biggest savings often come from simple changes, such as clearing sessions at the right time, tuning cache parameters or quietening chatty build scripts. Yet we often see developers reaching for complex solutions such as compression proxies without measuring their impact.

name: Enterprise harness
description: An enterprise harness An enterprise harness is the organization-wide layer of what coding agents consume managed collectively. It includes skills, tools, connectors to internal context, approved technologies, architecture decision records, path-to-production guidance, hooks and security policies. We observe that as multiple teams in an organization adopt coding agents, they need common context to complement each team's curated shared instructions. It's like a developer experience platform, but for agent experience. We've seen organizations go as far as building a custom coding agent on top of OpenCode, but we recommend sharing assets through open standards and distributing them via an agent plugin marketplace. There's no consensus yet on how to do this well, so keep the enterprise harness thin and federated, leave room for experimentation and harvest what works.
relatedBlips: Agent plugin marketplace;OpenCode;Lightweight Architecture Decision Records;Curated shared instructions for software teams

name: Foundation models for structured data
description:
Enterprise AI has focused heavily on text and vision, while much business data remains locked in relational databases. Foundation models adapt transformers to structured data, pretraining on an organization’s event sequences and transaction logs to learn reusable representations of business behavior.


Unlike traditional gradient-boosted models that require extensive feature engineering and retraining, these models can support multiple downstream tasks with lightweight fine-tuning. Tools such as TabPFN and TabFM can improve risk assessment, predictive analytics and customer retention directly from tabular or relational data. Given their potential to unlock business insights without complex feature pipelines, we suggest assessing this technique.

name: Harness quality evaluation
description:
Nowadays, organizations and teams come up with custom harnesses tailored to their projects, including agent skills, plugins, AGENTS.md and deterministic guardrails. Harness quality evaluation has become an important technique. Guardrails and harnesses help a coding agent course-correct and improve overall quality, but only if they actually work.


A harness usually includes both deterministic and non-deterministic components. For non-deterministic harnesses, our teams use PluginEval to evaluate coding agent plugins or skills. For deterministic harnesses, we introduce a test suite to enable TDD-style development of any guardrails, ensuring each one actually works and providing evidence of its effectiveness. We recommend running evaluations on a scheduled basis (such as nightly or alongside CI).

name: Local coding models
description:
In previous editions of the Radar, we put local coding assistants in Caution because the available models were too limited for complex software engineering contexts and weren’t a compelling solution to the concerns they were intended to address. With coding agents now being adopted much more widely than 18 months ago and local open-weight models maturing rapidly, our teams have found local coding models effective in addressing blanket frontier model usage.


Models that can run locally, such as Qwen3.8-27B, have proved particularly useful for workloads that don’t require a frontier model, including codebase indexing, structured log parsing and summarization, initial coding tasks and automated reviews of Git diffs and commits. Running these tasks locally can avoid incremental cloud token costs while also enabling long-running background processing and providing an offline fallback.

name: MITRE ATLAS
description:
Agentic systems and coding tools introduce new architectures and emergent security threats. MITRE ATLAS is a knowledge base of adversarial tactics and techniques targeting AI and ML systems. More focused than the broader MITRE ATT&CK framework and designed to complement it, ATLAS provides a taxonomy of threats for ML pipelines, LLM applications and agentic systems.


We've found that without a shared vocabulary, security risks are often overlooked or reduced to a checkbox exercise. This is where ATLAS can help. Grounded in research on real incidents and technology patterns, teams can use the framework to support threat modeling. Teams may also find it a natural complement to control frameworks such as SAIF, helping describe the evolving threat landscape for AI systems.

name: Production-aware coding agents
description: We've long said that being conscious of production helps developers write better code, and we're finding the same applies to coding agents. We recommend production-aware coding agents, which means giving coding agents appropriate access to production observability data and tools. This context helps them plan effective changes, review the impact of deployed changes and assist with investigating production issues. A growing tooling category is making this access practical. This recommendation is similar to agent pipeline responsibility, extending the feedback sensors that keep agents self-correcting during a coding session beyond pre-commit checks and into production. We believe successful development has multiple layers of feedback, and successful agentic engineering gives agents access to all of them.
relatedBlips: Agent pipeline responsibility;Feedback sensors for coding agents

name: Programmatic tool calling
description:
Programmatic tool calling is a tool-use pattern where the model writes code instead of issuing one tool call at a time. Rather than making a round-trip through the model for each operation, it combines tool calls into a program that runs in an execution environment, looping, filtering and shaping results. Only the selected results or the final output are returned to the model’s context.


The concept appears in several implementations, although the naming is still unsettled. Cloudflare and Pi call it Code Mode; Anthropic calls it programmatic tool calling; and an earlier Anthropic engineering article describes code execution with MCP. DeepSeek Harness (DSH) also provides a closely related PTC Mode.


Implementations differ mainly in where the execution environment runs: in a model provider’s container, the agent harness or, more recently, through a Code Mode MCP server. The latter allows MCP clients to use programmatic tool calling without implementing their own execution runtime. However, it can reduce the granularity of client-side approvals, so authorization and approval for individual operations must still be enforced by the server and its tool handlers.

name: Semantic review of AI-edited prose
description: Coding agents produce and revise prose artifacts such as specifications, ADRs and plans far faster than humans can review them. Text diffs bury intent under rewording and formatting noise, making it hard to see whether a plan has changed significantly. Semantic review of AI-edited prose adds a layer on top of the text diff: an LLM analyzes changes in meaning, such as altered facts, conflicting statements, redefined acceptance criteria and changes in scope. Much like automated PR review but for prose, it can be implemented as an agent skill that runs whenever a coding agent edits a document. We’ve seen Thoughtworks teams use this technique to reduce cognitive load and review fatigue, helping reviewers better understand changes to planned work before implementation.

name: Tests as data over tests as code
description:
Tests as data over tests as code means expressing test cases as structured data, typically YAML or JSON, rather than as test code. A project-specific test harness reads that data and executes the underlying code: the harness provides the building blocks, while the test cases define how they’re assembled. The technique isn't new; BDD with Gherkin is a prime example. What makes it relevant again is that AI coding agents now write more code, including tests. We’ve found that a defined schema better constrains what they produce, making tests easier to generate and review, with less AI-generated test code.


A few of our teams have also seen a compelling use case in legacy modernization, where the same test cases expressed as data can run against both legacy and modern code by swapping the harness adapter. This helps teams verify that the modernized system behaves like the original, at least for the cases covered by the tests. Using the technique with AI is still relatively new to us, and we haven't applied it broadly. However, the results so far are promising, and we think it's worth assessing.

name: Agent instruction bloat
description:
Instructions for coding agents, such as AGENTS.md guidance, process skills and workflows, tend to grow longer over time. Although each new rule might be useful in isolation, this accumulation often leads to agent instruction bloat. The instructions become long, contradictory and stale, especially if teams engage in agent skill cognitive surrender and import external instruction sets wholesale.


First, convert any instructions you can into deterministic hooks or checks. Then, reevaluate instructions against each new model and delete those it no longer needs; progression testing, rather than regression testing. Anthropic removed over 80% of Claude Code's system prompt for its latest models with no measurable loss, as frontier models now follow instructions more reliably. Progressive context disclosure keeps the remaining instructions out of the way until they’re needed.

name: Agent skill cognitive surrender
description:
There is a growing trend of agent skill cognitive surrender, an antipattern in which teams adopt large, community-curated skill libraries or heavyweight AI agent frameworks without fully understanding what they do. Much like blindly importing large software dependencies, developers can treat these skills as ready-made capabilities and lose sight of how the underlying system works. This isn't a new problem; similar examples include copy-pasting code without understanding it or over-relying on generic design patterns. However, the proliferation of AI tools has made the issue much more apparent.


Beyond the loss of system understanding, surrendering critical evaluation introduces security risks: unreviewed prompt instructions can make their way into execution pipelines. Skills from different sources may also conflict when they weren't designed to work together. It’s important to inspect and review skill instructions before adapting them rather than using general-purpose agent skills indiscriminately. As underlying models become more capable, generic community skills can become unnecessary or obsolete, making it more valuable to curate domain-specific skills tailored to a project's context.

name: AI-accelerated shadow IT
description: We observe many noncoders graduating from no-code platforms to coding agents such as Claude Code and OpenAI Codex. We celebrate people solving their own problems, but AI-accelerated shadow IT, whether built by noncoders or developers, comes with risks. First among these is security. Second, software originating from outside traditional development usually lacks testing, deployment pipelines and observability. This particularly matters if one person's productivity tool is adopted by their team or department. Organizations should prioritize governance with limits and guidelines on AI-generated applications. In our experience, it's better to provide colleagues with environments and enterprise harnesses for safe experimentation than to extinguish their enthusiasm. Be firm on security, and give useful tools a clear path to support.

name: AI-driven documentation sprawl
description:
AI-driven documentation sprawl occurs when teams use AI agents and spec-driven development tools such as Spec-kit or BMAD to generate large volumes of Markdown files and documentation. Because AI can produce polished, professional-looking docs in seconds, the result can create an illusion of software quality and rapid progress. Unlike source code, however, documentation rarely passes through automated quality gates or CI tests. As projects evolve, repositories rapidly accumulate verbose, unmaintained and contradictory specs that developers lack the time to clean up, resulting in a chaotic "big ball of documentation mud."


This overabundance of obsolete documentation is particularly problematic in agentic workflows. When coding agents read through a repository littered with outdated architectural decision records or conflicting specification files, these redundant and contradictory documents consume valuable context and provide unreliable information. Rather than aiding development, obsolete context can lead AI tools astray and result in poor code generation. To maintain agent effectiveness, teams must treat Markdown as a first-class artifact, spending deliberate human effort to prune, refine and consolidate generated context files so the agent’s context remains crisp, relevant and authoritative.

name: Blanket frontier model usage
description: We've sometimes caught ourselves defaulting every task that requires an LLM to the most capable model available, paying no attention to cost, latency or required capability. We call this blanket frontier model usage. Frontier models can cost significantly more and run more slowly than their more nimble counterparts; routine work such as exploration, simple edits or summarizing is often better served by a smaller model or even open-weight models. You can switch tiers manually, per subagent or through harness settings that switch automatically based on task complexity or stage. Each model has its own prompt cache, so you can also switch at natural boundaries, a new session, a subagent or the handoff from planning to implementation, rather than per request. A warning on our warning, though: more capable models sometimes finish tasks using fewer tokens, so use context profiling to check whether your optimization is working.
relatedBlips: Subagents for better context management;Open-weight models;Context profiling

name: Coding throughput as a measure of productivity
description:
In a previous Radar, we warned against using coding throughput as a measure of productivity. As the industry pushes for AI adoption and seeks tangible metrics, we increasingly see activity-based metrics such as the percentage of code generated by AI or tokens consumed treated as badges of honor. Although such metrics may indicate adoption levels, they’re poor proxies for real productivity gains.


To measure meaningful productivity, we continue to recommend established frameworks such as DORA metrics and collaboration quality, along with tying improvements directly to business outcomes. Treating activity metrics as targets rather than signals risks falling prey to Goodhart's law. We’ve seen developers generating AI busywork simply to hit these targets.
relatedBlips: DORA metrics;Measuring collaboration quality with coding agents

name: Human-in-the-loop theater
description:
Human-in-the-loop theater is keeping a human in an agent's loop as an empty approval step rather than a real check. The human approves actions, prompts or diffs they can't realistically evaluate.


The approval step functions as an accountability sink: no one truly owns the decision. Our advice is instead to triage. Reserve human review for changes a human can genuinely judge, using risk-tiered human oversight. For the rest, shift from reviewing individual changes to steering the system with mutation testing, property-based testing, formal models such as TLA+ and Quint and agent-assisted semantic review.
relatedBlips: Meat proxy;TLA+;Risk-tiered human oversight;Mutation testing;Semantic review of AI-edited prose;Quint

name: Meat proxy
description: A meat proxy is a person who unthinkingly passes on unverified LLM output to a colleague, forwarding it without reading, validating or adding substantive judgment. It's a violation of good AI etiquette and, in our unfortunate experience, a growing problem. When you act as a meat proxy, you shift the verification burden downstream onto the other person and shirk your own responsibility for assuring quality work. This is similar to human-in-the-loop theater, except that it's fake authorship instead of fake approval. In neither case is the human adding value. KDE's draft AI guidelines put it well: "Don't be a meat proxy."

name: Naive context compression
description:
As token costs rise, teams increasingly turn to tools like Headroom, RTK and Tamp to shrink their prompts. However, we advise against naive context compression, which can introduce several subtle problems. First, it often interferes with prompt caching; reducing token counts while missing cache hits can lead to higher actual bills. Second, aggressive compression causes information loss, degrading the performance and accuracy of agentic loops. Third, some tools rely on an LLM to summarize context during compression, adding latency and costs that defeat the purpose.


Before adopting these tools, profile your context usage and rigorously evaluate both net cost and task accuracy; token reduction means nothing if prompt caches break or agent performance degrades. Opt for tools that compress tool outputs while preserving references to the raw data and that prune history only in one shot at task boundaries, to protect cache prefixes.

name: Stacked pull requests
description:
Stacked pull requests break a large change into an ordered chain of small, dependent pull requests (PRs). Rather than targeting the main repository branch, each subsequent PR targets the branch directly below it in the stack. We've seen a surge in interest in this technique recently due to the rapid adoption of AI-assisted coding tools. Teams adopt this approach to reduce review latency and developer idle time. By evaluating small, isolated layers, reviewers face lower cognitive overhead. Tooling has also improved to support this workflow; GitHub recently introduced native support.


Despite better tooling, we've placed this technique in the Caution ring because it’s often a workaround for poor upfront decomposition. Stacking doesn't create decomposition problems; it exposes ones that were already there. The risk isn't the technique itself; it's using it as a substitute for that planning. Habitual, undifferentiated stacking can easily become an excuse to write one enormous change. We maintain that the better habit is to specify, split, size and deliver work as small, independent units.

name: VictoriaMetrics
description:
We've moved VictoriaMetrics to Adopt because it has matured into a reliable choice for organizations operating large-scale, self-managed observability platforms. As a high-performance, open-source time-series database, it handles high-volume and high-cardinality metrics workloads that can challenge Prometheus. In one of our projects, a VictoriaMetrics cluster handles five million samples per second with 20 to 30 labels per metric, demonstrating its suitability for large-scale deployments.


The platform offers a straightforward single-node version for smaller workloads as well as a clustered architecture that separates ingestion, querying and storage into independently scalable components. It integrates with existing observability architectures by supporting native OpenTelemetry ingestion, Prometheus APIs and remote write support, allowing teams to adopt it without replacing their existing instrumentation and dashboards. Whether used as long-term storage behind Prometheus or as a complete metrics stack with components such as vmagent and vmalert, VictoriaMetrics is a compelling option for infrastructure where retention, cardinality or cost has become a challenge.

name: Kafka share groups
description:
Kafka share groups (introduced in KIP-932, production-ready since Kafka v4.2) bring a new cooperative event consumption model to Kafka, enabling queue-like behavior. Historically, Kafka's traditional consumer groups have imposed a concurrency bottleneck because the number of active consumers can’t exceed the number of partitions. Share groups remove this constraint: individual records are handed to any available consumer in the pool under a per-record acquisition lock, which the consumer must explicitly acknowledge. On failure or timeout, the record is released and redelivered to any consumer in the group, up to a configurable maximum number of delivery attempts. This provides at-least-once delivery with the possibility of duplicate-processing. Records that exhaust their delivery attempts are archived; dead-letter queue support (KIP-1191) is not yet available.


The tradeoff is that share groups don’t guarantee per-partition ordering because records are dispatched and redelivered independently. However, for teams that previously had to run both Kafka and an external queue system, share groups can simplify the architecture by consolidating workloads onto Kafka.

name: KServe
description:
KServe is an open-source Kubernetes operator that manages predictive and generative AI inference through custom resources. Rather than acting as an inference engine itself, it orchestrates serving runtimes such as vLLM, SGLang and NVIDIA Triton, separating the lifecycle of a model service from the engine that executes it.


As organizations build AI factories, operating inference across Kubernetes GPU infrastructure becomes a fleet-management problem rather than a matter of running individual model servers. KServe addresses this with two custom resources: InferenceService for conventional machine learning and simpler LLM workloads, with optional Knative-based scale-to-zero, and LLMInferenceService for advanced LLM serving. Built on llm-d and the Gateway API Inference Extension, LLMInferenceService supports multi-node inference, prefill/decode disaggregation and KV-cache-aware routing that directs requests to replicas already holding the relevant cached prefix.


KServe is a CNCF incubating project, and several of our clients use it in production. Our teams prefer it over other tools in this space when building in-house inference platforms on Kubernetes. LLMInferenceService is newer than InferenceService, and its ecosystem is still evolving.

name: LibreChat
description:
LibreChat is an open-source, self-hosted AI chat platform that lets people across an organization access models from multiple providers through a single interface. Like Open WebUI, it offers single sign-on, role-based permissions and RAG over uploaded documents. Its agent features make it more than a chat frontend. Administrators decide which MCP servers are available. Users whose role allows it can then build agents on those servers without writing code and share them through a built-in marketplace.


One of our teams built a client's internal AI platform on LibreChat. The team wrote MCP servers for Jira, Confluence, Salesforce, Grafana and the client's own order, inventory and revenue systems. The client's staff then built the agents themselves: sales created one to check availability and book orders, while operations built one to manage contracts. That experience is why we're placing it in Trial. It gives people outside engineering a controlled way to access vetted AI tooling, which is what we've recommended as the answer to AI-accelerated shadow IT. ClickHouse acquired LibreChat in November 2025, and the project remains MIT licensed.
relatedBlips: AI-accelerated shadow IT;ClickHouse;Open WebUI;Grafana;Model Context Protocol (MCP)

name: LiteLLM
description:
LiteLLM has become a widely used open-source AI gateway. Several of our teams route their model calls through it, either as a standalone proxy or as a sidecar. It supports more than 100 LLM providers and offers routing, provider translation, authentication, budgets and guardrails. Its proxy core is being rewritten from Python to Rust to improve performance while retaining the same Python SDK and configuration.


We’re moving LiteLLM from Languages and Frameworks to Platforms in this edition because we now see it more as infrastructure than a library. We’re keeping it in Trial rather than Adopt largely because of security concerns: at the time of writing, more than 25 CVEs have been reported this year alone. Teams using it should apply security patches promptly. To also govern MCP and agent-to-agent traffic, consider combining it with agentgateway.

name: Microsoft Copilot Retrieval API
description: Microsoft Copilot Retrieval API is a streamlined solution for retrieving data from the Microsoft ecosystem for retrieval-augmented generation (RAG). The API retrieves relevant text extracts from SharePoint, OneDrive and content exposed through Copilot connectors. It applies security trimming based on the calling user and respects access controls defined within the tenant. Developers can build organization-aware AI agents without maintaining custom data stores and retrieval pipelines, leaving tasks such as chunking, indexing, data synchronization, reindexing and access control to Microsoft. The Microsoft Copilot Retrieval API is particularly useful for AI systems that need organizational knowledge already stored in Microsoft tools, and we’ve had a positive experience adopting it.

name: Restate
description:
Restate is a durable execution platform for building stateful, fault-tolerant applications. Because it journals every step of execution, a service that fails resumes where it left off. Restate also guarantees exactly-once communication between services. An application combines Basic Services for stateless functions, Virtual Objects for concurrent stateful entities and Workflows for multi-step processes.


When we last wrote about Restate, we were assessing it on a large insurance system. It's now a core part of that system, automating an entire insurance business process. The team relies on its state recovery and concurrency control and hasn't had to write its own recovery code. That experience is why we're moving it to Trial. Restate suits long-running processes that wait on a human in the loop or retry many times against legacy systems. It fills the same role as Temporal, which also moves to Trial in this edition. The SDKs are MIT licensed, but the server uses the Business Source License, which rules out offering it to third parties as a managed service.

name: Talos Linux
description:
Talos Linux is a minimal, immutable Linux distribution for running Kubernetes. It has no SSH, package manager or interactive shell. You configure nodes declaratively with talosctl through an mTLS-secured gRPC API, and upgrades replace the entire OS image. This design reduces the attack surface and configuration drift associated with general-purpose distributions such as Ubuntu and makes each node a replaceable appliance, in the spirit of immutable servers.


One of our teams runs self-managed Kubernetes on Talos across a large bare-metal fleet for an AI cloud platform and found the control plane easy to provision. Most organizations use a managed service such as Amazon EKS and never interact with the node OS, so Talos is primarily for teams that operate their own nodes. Bottlerocket takes a similar approach on AWS, and Flatcar Container Linux also has traction. In 2026, Yardi acquired Sidero Labs, the developer of Talos. Talos remains open source under MPL-2.0, but teams should watch where the new owner takes it.

name: Temporal
description:
Temporal is a durable execution platform for complex business processes that require strong reliability guarantees. Temporal provides workflows with retries, intermediate state persistence, configurable timeouts, human-in-the-loop checkpoints, resumability and visibility into execution progress. It offers both an open-source self-hosted option and a managed cloud service.


We’ve found compelling use cases for Temporal when building internal developer platforms and control planes for AI cloud infrastructure. These systems typically involve multiple long-running infrastructure provisioning tasks whose state must be reconciled later. Temporal's built-in retries, flexible worker queue scheduling, resumability, visibility and durable execution help teams build these types of systems more resiliently.

name: vCluster
description:
vCluster provides virtualized Kubernetes control planes for multi-tenant environments. It offers a middle ground between namespace-level multi-tenancy, where tenants share cluster-wide APIs and custom resource definitions (CRDs), and provisioning completely independent clusters, which increases operational overhead. With vCluster, each tenant gets its own Kubernetes API server, controller manager, data store, RBAC and CRDs. The control plane runs as a lightweight workload on the underlying infrastructure, allowing standard tools such as kubectl, Helm and GitOps controllers to interact with each tenant independently.


We've successfully used vCluster to build managed Kubernetes services and AI cloud environments where balancing tenant isolation against operational costs is critical. It’s particularly attractive for AI platforms where different customers may need their own GPU operators, schedulers, inference frameworks and CRDs. For trusted workloads, virtualized control planes can share underlying compute resources. For customer-facing GPU environments, dedicated worker nodes can provide stronger workload isolation while retaining consolidated control plane management. Given its success in production client environments, we're placing vCluster in Trial.

name: VictoriaLogs
description:
Developed by the creators of VictoriaMetrics, VictoriaLogs is an open-source log management platform optimized for high-throughput ingestion, compact storage and fast querying of large log volumes. Rather than requiring predefined indexes, its storage engine organizes and compresses log fields into blocks. It uses Bloom filters and timestamp indexes to avoid unnecessary scans and parallelizes queries across CPU cores.


We've had positive experiences using VictoriaLogs while building observability for an AI cloud infrastructure system. At this scale, Kubernetes services generate large volumes of telemetry, making ingestion throughput, query performance and storage efficiency critical considerations. Compared with traditional search-based logging platforms like Elasticsearch, VictoriaLogs offers a capable logging backend with less operational complexity and lower resource overhead. We've also found it particularly attractive for high-cardinality structured logs and arbitrary field searches when compared with Grafana Loki, because it doesn't require the same degree of label design. VictoriaLogs also includes the LogsQL query language for full-text search, transformations and aggregation. It integrates with Grafana for interactive exploration and alerting, while compatibility with OpenTelemetry, Elasticsearch and Loki ingestion protocols allows teams to adopt it without tying applications to a proprietary logging pipeline.

name: Agent Client Protocol (ACP)
description:
While CLI-based coding agents excel at repo-wide implementation and workflow execution, developers still need inline access to agents within their IDEs for rapid code exploration, interactive bug fixing and context-aware editing. Traditionally, this requires individual IDE plugins, creating integration overhead and locking developers into specific editor-agent pairings. Agent Client Protocol (ACP) addresses this by establishing an open, standard boundary between AI agents and host environments, whether that’s VS Code, JetBrains, a terminal window or a CI/CD pipeline.


Much like the Language Server Protocol standardized language support across editors, ACP relies on JSON-RPC to define agent lifecycle and interaction primitives, including session creation and resumption, streaming updates, permission requests and cancellation. ACP complements existing interoperability layers: while the Model Context Protocol (MCP) handles agent-to-tool integration, ACP handles client-to-agent control, making the complete agent harness a swappable component.

name: Agent Plugins
description: Agent Plugins is an open standard for packaging reusable agent components into portable plugins. The first version, launched by a cross-vendor collaboration including Amazon, Microsoft and OpenAI, defines a shared format for agent skills and Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers. Although the specification is deliberately minimal, an open standard is an important step forward for an ecosystem that has so far been fragmented. We've found that the "small interoperability floor" makes it easy to extend an existing skills repository so that it doubles as an Agent Plugin.

name: agentgateway
description:
agentgateway is a high-performance gateway for LLM-related traffic, hosted by the Linux Foundation. It supports LLM inference, MCP and A2A communication through a common protocol in both standalone and Kubernetes versions. Core features include cost- and latency-based routing, fallbacks, spending limits, guardrails, MCP tool control and OpenTelemetry observability.


We’re particularly interested in the Kubernetes version because of its deep integration with self-hosted LLM infrastructure. It can use Kubernetes metrics to route requests to a GPU-backed replica that already has the relevant context cached in memory or to a less utilized server based on actual GPU usage. These capabilities make agentgateway worth evaluating for organizations running self-hosted inference stacks.

name: AWS DevOps Agent
description:
AWS DevOps Agent is a managed AWS agent platform for AI-driven incident investigation. When an alarm, ticket or chat message triggers an investigation, the platform maps application resources and their relationships, correlates telemetry with recent deployments and code changes, tests hypotheses and presents likely root causes and mitigations for an engineer to act on. Built-in integrations with Datadog, Dynatrace, New Relic, Splunk and Grafana let alerts from those tools trigger investigations and allow the platform to query their telemetry through MCP-based integrations. Connections to GitHub, GitLab, ServiceNow, PagerDuty and Slack, along with custom MCP servers, extend its reach to on-premises and proprietary systems.


Our teams are experimenting with it in production to investigate live alarms. It's early, but the results look promising, suggesting the potential for faster root-cause analysis and less operational toil. Our main reservation is cost transparency. The platform charges per agent-second spent investigating an incident, making costs difficult to predict. Spending can add up quickly without close monitoring. The service has only been generally available since March 2026, so we recommend assessing it with human validation of every finding, tight control over which events trigger investigations and active cost tracking.

name: Claude Managed Agents
description:
Claude Managed Agents is Anthropic's hosted service for running general-purpose agents. Teams define each agent's model, prompt, tools, MCP servers and skills. Anthropic provides the rest of a managed agents runtime: the agent loop, sandbox, scheduling and observability. Agents run on a schedule or when an application starts a session through the API. Scheduled runs are suited to recurring background work, such as triaging alerts and proposing fixes as pull requests for human review.


Teams can get started without writing code through the console or use code-based integrations for greater flexibility and control. Agent, environment and schedule definitions can be stored in files applied through a CI pipeline. A credential vault injects credentials into outbound requests without exposing them to the agent. One of our internal teams chose Claude Managed Agents over other agent platforms, including Gemini Enterprise Agent Platform, because it was easier to understand and faster to deliver with.


We're placing it in Assess because our experience is limited to that team and the service is in beta. Unlike Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, it supports only Anthropic's agent harness and Claude models. Anthropic charges for session runtime as well as tokens. Because the service stores sessions, it isn't eligible for Zero Data Retention. Self-hosted sandboxes can keep tool execution within your network, but orchestration and tool results still pass through Anthropic.

name: Decision models
description: A new class of AI models called decision models has emerged since the last Radar. TypeSafe AI released Jev, which it calls a "system one" model, built to make fast, structured decisions. Many other models have followed, including Laya, Nimble and Kev. In contrast to deliberative reasoning models, decision models output predefined structured values instead of generated text. Rather than using reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) to optimize for human preferences, Jev uses reinforcement learning from calibrated decisions (RLCD) to optimize for well-calibrated decisions, where predicted probabilities reflect how often an outcome actually occurs. Their smaller, structured outputs enable faster and cheaper processing. Decision models receive a state and a set of questions. Every question asked against the state must map to one of three types: Noul for yes/no questions that return the probability of a "yes" answer, Choice for categorized multiple-choice options or Score for evaluations on an ordered list of levels or a numerical scale. Decision model use cases include Jev-as-a-judge as an alternative to LLM-as-a-judge, model and tool routing, policy gates and bulk labeling. We recommend teams avoid overenthusiastic LLM use and define evaluation criteria to determine whether a decision model can replace an LLM for classification use cases.
relatedBlips: LLM as a judge;Overenthusiastic LLM use

name: KAITO
description:
KAITO (Kubernetes AI Toolchain Operator) is a Kubernetes operator that automates the infrastructure needed to self-host open-weight models on your own clusters. Instead of manually configuring GPU nodes and model servers, teams declare a Workspace, KAITO's custom resource for a single model deployment, specifying the model and GPU instance type. The KAITO controller then provisions matching GPU nodes through Karpenter NodePools, estimates GPU memory requirements, tunes the runtime and serves the model through vLLM, exposing an OpenAI-compatible endpoint via a Kubernetes Service.


Our teams began exploring KAITO on AKS to host small language models at lower cost and latency. Previously, running Ollama and vLLM directly on GPU VMs had left them managing drivers, scaling and node configuration manually. Managing the model lifecycle through the same declarative manifests as other workloads promises to reduce much of that toil.


KAITO's scope is deliberately narrow, though. It handles node provisioning and model deployment rather than the broader inference stack, where KServe is more mature and offers capabilities such as KV-cache-aware routing. KAITO is still a CNCF Sandbox project. Its GPU node auto-provisioning is most mature on AKS, and it supports only Ampere-generation or newer NVIDIA GPUs. We think it's worth assessing, particularly for teams that want to self-host models using their existing Kubernetes tooling.

name: llm-d
description:
llm-d is an open-source distributed inference serving stack designed to operate model servers such as vLLM and SGLang across multiple Kubernetes nodes. Traditional web applications often rely on stateless routing and horizontal scaling, but LLM inference is highly stateful due to key value (KV) caching. Rather than treating model-serving pods as interchangeable HTTP backends, llm-d uses inference-aware routing to coordinate requests across multiple accelerators, extending optimization beyond individual model servers.


Built around Kubernetes and the Gateway API Inference Extension, llm-d offers several capabilities tailored to stateful AI traffic. It supports model-aware and KV-cache-aware routing, using factors such as cache affinity, queue depth and predicted latency to guide scheduling decisions. A notable feature is prefill and decode disaggregation, which allows operators to place compute-intensive prefill workloads on one set of GPUs and memory-bandwidth-bound decoding tasks on another. This can improve hardware utilization and reduce inference costs. Teams building large-scale GPU inference platforms should assess llm-d as an emerging foundation for their inference layer, particularly when looking to scale while meeting strict latency objectives.

name: Netris
description:
Netris is an out-of-band network automation and multi-tenancy platform for physical data centers and AI infrastructure. Using a declarative, infrastructure-as-code model accessible through a UI, an API, Kubernetes CRDs and Terraform, it simplifies network management by abstracting switch configurations into cloud-style virtual private clouds (VPCs), virtual networks, access control lists (ACLs) and Layer 4 load balancers. A central controller manages policies while lightweight agents execute changes on switches and data processing units (DPUs). The controller operates out-of-band as an automation control plane, so packet forwarding can continue uninterrupted even if the controller goes offline.


We’re highlighting Netris for its support of high-bandwidth AI workloads. It automates routed Ethernet VPN (EVPN) fabrics, manages flow control for RDMA over Converged Ethernet (RoCE) and orchestrates NVIDIA BlueField DPUs for hardware-enforced multi-tenancy. It also integrates with NVIDIA UFM for InfiniBand partition keys (PKeys) and NMX-C for NVLink domains, helping manage multi-tenant boundaries across different AI fabrics through a unified management layer. We’re placing Netris in Assess for teams building automated private clouds or AI data centers, although teams should evaluate compatibility with their switch operating systems, such as SONiC, Cumulus Linux and Arista EOS, as well as the boundaries of bare-metal orchestration support.

name: Omnigent
description:
Omnigent is an open-source meta-harness, released by Databricks, that sits above coding agents such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex and Pi, as well as agents defined in YAML. It provides a common layer for capabilities that each harness otherwise implements differently. Policies can cap spending or require approval before a risky action, while an OS sandbox restricts file system and network access and swaps credentials into outgoing requests, so the agent can use them without reading them. Sessions persist, allowing a run to resume where it stopped. Omnigent can also communicate with agents through the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) instead of wrapping each CLI.


On a laptop, Omnigent gives a developer an inbox of parallel sessions, much as Herdr does. As a shared server, it adds single sign-on, live session sharing and administrator-set policies, with sessions running locally or in cloud sandboxes such as E2B. This suits organizations that want consistent controls regardless of which coding agents their developers choose. We aren't yet sure what the right abstraction over coding agents is, and the project still describes itself as alpha. Teams that want consistent policies across several coding agents should evaluate Omnigent with both caveats in mind.

name: VAST DataStore
description:
VAST DataStore is the storage layer of the VAST Data platform. It provides file (NFS and SMB), object (S3) and block (NVMe/TCP) access through a unified namespace. Its disaggregated shared-everything architecture separates stateless compute nodes from shared NVMe storage, allowing capacity and performance to scale independently. We're assessing it because storage throughput increasingly affects how efficiently expensive GPU clusters operate during training, checkpointing and model loading. DataStore lets workloads retain conventional NFS/POSIX or S3 access while using NVMe and RDMA for faster data transfer, offering an alternative to specialized parallel file systems. VAST is also working with NVIDIA on S3 over RDMA and shared KV-cache storage for disaggregated inference.


Compared with Ceph, which offers open-source block, file and object storage on commodity hardware, DataStore is a proprietary platform designed for NVMe, RDMA and AI workloads. However, it’s expensive and ties you to VAST's broader data platform, so it may be more than teams need unless they're training models or running large-scale inference. We think VAST DataStore is worth assessing for teams designing large GPU clusters for AI and high-performance computing (HPC) workloads, where data loading, checkpointing and metadata-heavy access to billions of files can leave expensive GPUs waiting on storage.

name: mise
description:
Since our last assessment, mise has evolved from a high-performance alternative to asdf into a default frontend for the development environment. We’re keeping it in Adopt because it consolidates three fragmented concerns (tool and language versioning, environment variable management and task execution) into a single high-performance, Rust-based tool, configured through a declarative mise.toml file. mise is easy to set up and works well with CI/CD pipelines. It also adds a layer of supply chain security through integration with Cosign and GitHub artifact attestations, which is often missing from other version managers.


For teams looking to standardize their developer environment setup, mise has become our recommended default. In polyglot environments with multiple microservices, this is especially useful when codebases adopt new language versions at the same time. Best of all, mise also works with existing language-specific tooling, so teams do not need to migrate all at once.

name: OpenAI Codex
description: OpenAI Codex moves to Adopt, joining Claude Code and OpenCode as CLI-first coding agents our teams use day to day. Its desktop app is popular with non-coders. Codex has the features you'd expect for enterprise adoption: OS-level sandboxing, tiered approvals, central configuration and compliance management. The underlying agent loop is Apache-2.0 licensed and can be used for the technique we call coding harness for general-purpose agents. Although open source, Codex is corporate-run rather than community-governed. It employs the classic challenger's gambit of compatibility: it makes it easy to import configuration, skills and sessions from other agents and to use models besides OpenAI's GPTs. That makes Codex a solid choice for running open-weight models.
relatedBlips: Coding harness for general-purpose agents;OpenCode;Open-weight models;Claude Code

name: OpenCode
description: Since our last Radar, OpenCode remains one of the most prominent open-source coding agent harnesses. We’ve seen its adoption grow significantly alongside the rise of capable open-weight models. Teams appreciate its customizability and headless/server mode, which make it an attractive foundation for organizations building an enterprise harness. On the downside, its session-sharing and collaboration capabilities still lag behind competing harnesses. OpenCode has become a popular choice for teams pairing coding agents with self-hosted, open-weight models and local coding models, but we still recommend evaluating emerging alternatives such as Pi.

name: Act
description:
Act runs GitHub Actions workflows locally, replacing the commit–push–wait loop with faster feedback. We mentioned it in our GitHub Actions blip back in 2021. Coding agents give Act new relevance because the growing volume of commits and pushes can cause build contention. Act lets coding agents run a workflow locally before pushing, bringing CI directly into their generative loop and supporting agent pipeline responsibility.


Our teams find that Act handles most GitHub Actions workflow development, although it isn't a perfect replica of the GitHub Actions environment. For example, its default images lack some runner tools, and it doesn’t support concurrency, permissions and environment secrets. Paired with static checking such as zizmor, Act helps coding agents keep the build working when they change the pipeline itself.

name: Agent Package Manager
description: Agent Package Manager is an open-source dependency manager for AI agent configuration. It works via a manifest that declares plugins, skills, instructions and MCP servers. We use it to publish versioned skills from a central repository instead of copy-pasting files around. It treats agent context as a supply chain, installing from Git repos or an agent plugin marketplace and scanning for hidden Unicode that could hijack behavior. Its lock files record content hashes and provenance, while its SBOMs export to CycloneDX and SPDX formats. Auditing detects drift, and a policy file constrains sources, scopes and primitives, making an enterprise harness reproducible and governed. It's still a pre-1.0, community-driven project, albeit one sponsored by a major player, so we place it in Trial rather than Adopt and expect competing solutions to follow.
