name: ast-grep
description:
ast-grep is a command-line tool for structural code search, linting and rewriting. Patterns are written as ordinary code with wildcards for any syntax node and match against the syntax tree rather than text, using tree-sitter parsers for more than 20 languages. Linting and rewriting rules are written in a declarative YAML format. One of our teams used these rules as part of the harness around a coding agent, checking the agent’s code against a set of custom rules and feeding the results back to the agent.


ast-grep is similar to the tools behind code intelligence as agentic tooling, but it doesn't build an index or require a language server. Because it skips indexing, it's a low-friction first step for a large codebase before committing to heavier tools. Unlike most tools in that group, it also has uses that don't involve agents: developers can run the same searches, lint rules and rewrites themselves. ast-grep covers much the same ground as Comby, which we featured in 2021. Most IDEs already offer AST-based search, but they don't replace the custom lint rules and rewrites that set ast-grep apart.

name: Beads
description:
Beads is a Git-backed issue tracker that coding agents can share to coordinate their work. In place of ad hoc Markdown plans, it gives agents a persistent, structured task graph. Because Beads stores tasks and their dependencies alongside the code, agents retain their plans and newly discovered tasks across sessions and context compaction. Each agent can claim the next available task without colliding with others.


We're moving Beads to Trial because many of our developers now use it by default with coding agents. It complements team issue trackers such as Linear, which teams use to plan, prioritize and track work. Beads holds the finer-grained tasks agents create as they work, and it syncs both ways with Linear, Jira and GitHub Issues.


Since we last featured it, Beads has reached 1.0 and moved to the Gas Town Hall organization. It’s maintained by Gas City, the company behind Gas Town. Dolt is now its only storage backend, and additions such as an HTTP API, work leases and synchronization between stores make Beads heavier than the lightweight tracker it started as. Upgrades migrate the schema in place, and clients running different versions can't share a store, so teams should pin a single version for each shared store and review the instructions Beads writes into AGENTS.md.

name: Chaos Mesh
description: Chaos Mesh is an open-source Chaos Engineering toolkit for injecting controlled failures into cloud-native systems. Chaos Mesh defines fault simulations as declarative Kubernetes custom resources, allowing teams to use familiar tooling and manage chaos experiments through version control. We've found that its range of simulated failure scenarios, reproducibility and blast radius controls make it suitable for repeatable, automated testing at scale. This includes environments with GPU-dense AI infrastructure, where validating resilience can be particularly challenging but important.

name: Cube Core
description:
As analytics data is increasingly consumed by both custom applications and AI agents, defining metrics directly in dashboards or individual SQL queries often leads to duplication and metric drift. Cube Core is an open-source semantic layer that addresses this challenge by allowing teams to define metrics, dimensions, joins and access rules as code. By creating a governed, reusable semantic model, teams can define business metrics once and expose them consistently across BI tools, embedded analytics and AI workflows through standard APIs.


We've used Cube Core successfully to implement a semantic layer in recent projects. The tool has an active codebase and contributor community. If you're struggling with inconsistent data definitions across multiple consumption layers, we recommend evaluating Cube Core to standardize analytics access.

name: Figma Code Connect
description:
Generic design-to-code tools often turn frames into raw markup that ignores a team's existing components, resulting in code that needs to be rewritten. Figma Code Connect addresses this disconnect by mapping Figma components directly to production UI components in code. Instead of guessing component APIs, AI tools and developers can use these mappings to generate code with your actual component signatures and props. This structured approach grounds code generation in the existing design system.


This tool is particularly relevant as teams move from prompt-based code generation to more controlled, agentic workflows. By pairing Figma Code Connect with the Figma MCP server and coding agents, developers can provide agents with context from the actual codebase. This helps shift free-form code generation toward more deterministic, production-compliant component assembly, reducing code review iterations and the risk of architectural drift.


In our experience with mobile design systems, we've used this workflow to map components across iOS and Android, auto-publishing to Figma after main-branch releases and using continuous integration (CI) to detect drift. However, Figma-to-code generation is only as reliable as the underlying design system. Generated output still requires guardrails, such as lint checks to block hardcoded colors and snapshot baselines on every pull request. Maintaining mappings for every variant also requires ongoing effort, and the tool currently operates at the component level rather than validating complete product screens. Layout logic, state and navigation therefore still require human oversight.

name: FluxMarkdown
description:
FluxMarkdown is a macOS QuickLook plugin that renders Markdown files directly in the Finder preview panel. While other options like QLMarkdown exist, FluxMarkdown offers comprehensive support for syntax highlighting, mathematical notations via KaTeX and complex diagrams using Mermaid, Graphviz and Vega.


We've found FluxMarkdown useful for inspecting documentation because it eliminates the need to open a dedicated editor just to view a rendered diagram or equation. As developers increasingly rely on command-line interfaces and autonomous agents in their workflows, viewing rendered Markdown files can still require opening an IDE. FluxMarkdown provides a lightweight alternative that lets developers preview these files without leaving Finder.

name: Git AI
description:
Git AI is an open-source Git extension designed to track AI-generated code in repositories. It links AI-written lines to the agents, models and prompts that generated them. Using checkpoints and hooks, the tool tracks incremental code changes throughout development. Each checkpoint contains a diff between the current state and the previous one, marking lines as either human- or AI-authored. This approach provides more detailed attribution of AI contributions than simply counting lines of code at the time they’re added.


The extension uses an open standard based on git notes to track AI-generated code. As AI-generated code becomes more common in everyday development, maintaining accountability and understanding the original intent behind code becomes increasingly important. Both developers and AI agents can query archived sessions to retrieve the original context and design decisions. Given its potential value for accountability and maintainability in agentic workflows, we’ve moved Git AI to Trial.

name: Linear
description: Linear is an issue tracker that pairs the easy setup of Trello with the planning features teams usually turn to Jira for. Many startups have used it in place of Jira for years, and its recent appeal comes from how well it works with coding agents. Agents join a Linear workspace as members, so teams can assign them issues, mention them in comments and see the reasoning behind each change. Cursor, OpenAI Codex and Devin can all take on work this way, while Linear's remote MCP server lets tools such as Claude Code read and update issues. Linear holds the work a team plans and prioritizes. Beads sits a level below it, tracking the smaller tasks agents create as they go. We often use Linear with clients whose teams work heavily with coding agents. Teams that choose their own tooling should consider trialing it if they want agents to pick up work directly from the backlog.

name: mattpocock/skills
description: mattpocock/skills ("Skills For Real Engineers") is a collection of agent skills for agentic software engineering. The skills provide a suggested workflow but are explicitly designed to be small, easy to adapt, and composable. We’ve found them valuable for helping teams apply sound software engineering practices to agentic coding, as well as for AI-assisted analysis of requirements and assumptions, such as grilling. While we caution against adopting entire skill libraries without evaluating them (agent skill cognitive surrender), these lightweight skills are worth a look if you want more structure in your agentic software development workflows.

name: OpenSpec
description: OpenSpec is a lightweight spec-driven development framework that works with any coding agent. Since we featured it in Assess in April, several of our teams have reported success with it, enough to move it to Trial. We particularly appreciate how it works on brownfield codebases, retrofitting specs onto existing code. Teams report more predictable agent output and fewer unintended changes compared to bare prompting. OpenSpec's key differentiator over competitors like GitHub Spec Kit and Kiro is that it centers on a spec-anchored workflow. Changes are deltas against a persistent source-of-truth spec, so agents can rely on it as a current reference. The usual caution applies: spec files are Markdown that agents generate prolifically. OpenSpec's archiving of change deltas mitigates this, but maintaining the persistent spec still requires discipline.
relatedBlips: AI-driven documentation sprawl;Spec-driven development;GitHub Spec Kit

name: OpenWiki
description:
OpenWiki is a command-line interface that automatically writes and maintains a wiki for a codebase or personal knowledge repository. It synthesizes source materials into a linked Markdown wiki that other agents can use as context. OpenWiki is currently in our Trial ring as we evaluate its impact on active projects. Our experience has reinforced a familiar challenge: high-quality documentation is essential, but keeping it up to date is notoriously difficult. OpenWiki addresses this by using automated pipelines to update content as source material changes, with checkpointing to track when each piece of documentation was last generated.


OpenWiki also supports local models for private generation and the OKF format for structured documentation. For humans, it includes an interactive visualizer that presents the underlying wiki as an explorable node graph, helping them navigate and understand relationships across interconnected topics and codebase documents.

name: Pi
description:
Pi is a minimal, open-source agent harness written in TypeScript. This blip covers the whole toolkit: the multi-provider LLM API (pi-ai), the agent runtime (pi-agent-core) and the terminal coding agent built on them (pi-coding-agent). Pi deliberately leaves out MCP, subagents, plan mode and permission prompts. You add what you need through extensions, agent skills and prompt templates. Pi can even write its own extensions. We're moving Pi to Trial because adoption has grown since the last Radar, mostly as a foundation for other tools. Security scanners and orchestration harnesses now run on Pi, often as an underlying dependency rather than a directly used tool, while its SDK and RPC modes let you embed it in other agent systems.


As a coding agent used directly, Pi isn't the strongest choice, and OpenCode is better suited as an enterprise coding harness. Oh My Pi, a popular fork, adds language server integration, subagents and MCP to create a full coding agent, but it has diverged enough to evaluate as a separate tool. Our concern last time was Pi’s dependence on one maintainer; in April 2026, its creator joined Earendil, which now owns Pi and has committed to keeping the core MIT-licensed while planning commercial add-ons.

name: Sourcebot
description: Just as developers need broad context across large, multi-repository enterprise codebases, software engineering agents need the same context to perform large-scale refactoring and navigate legacy ecosystems. Sourcebot is a self-hosted code search and understanding platform that acts as a context layer to serve both. It indexes thousands of repositories to provide fast, symbol-aware search and IDE-level navigation. With the Sourcebot MCP server, agents can search across an organization’s entire codebase. Our teams have also found the paid-tier feature Ask Sourcebot useful for team collaboration. This AI chat tool enables non-developer roles to query the codebase using natural language, reducing their reliance on developers to answer codebase questions.
relatedBlips: Software engineering agents;Using GenAI to understand legacy codebases;Sourcegraph

name: Timefold Solver
description: Timefold Solver is an open-source constraint optimization engine for Java and Kotlin and the modern successor to OptaPlanner. It solves logistical planning problems, such as vehicle routing, employee rostering, task assignment and maintenance scheduling, where the space of possibilities is far too large to search exhaustively. Although branded under the broader AI umbrella, it involves no training data or learned model, relying instead on heuristic search over constraints you define. It models absolute business rules as hard constraints that a returned plan can’t violate and operational targets as soft constraints that it optimizes within. We’ve successfully used Timefold Solver in production in the supply chain domain to rapidly model complex business scenarios.

name: AgentsView
description: As AI-assisted coding becomes mainstream, AgentsView gives developers observability into coding sessions so they can analyze patterns and improve harness usage. AgentsView lets developers browse, search and perform context profiling on past AI coding sessions. It can automatically hook into popular coding harnesses, such as Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, OpenCode or Pi and retrieve historical sessions. It includes coding session analysis tools for metrics such as prompt-cache and cost efficiency, along with recommendations for improving harness usage. One thing we like about AgentsView is its local-first design, which makes adoption straightforward even for security-conscious organizations, while team synchronization and collaborative session reviews can be added later.

name: Apple container
description: Apple container is an open-source tool for running Linux containers natively on Apple silicon. Written in Swift, it uses Apple’s Containerization package to run a lightweight VM for each container rather than a monolithic Linux VM. This architecture provides hypervisor-level isolation and dynamic memory allocation, returning RAM to macOS when a container is torn down. It offers a native, lightweight alternative to shared-VM managers such as Colima and avoids the licensing requirements associated with Docker Desktop. When paired with community bridges such as Socktainer for Docker API compatibility, Apple container is particularly effective for local Testcontainers setups that require fast cold starts and strict resource boundaries. The project also includes Container Machine for running persistent, host-integrated Linux environments.

name: Deepsec
description: Deepsec is an agent-powered vulnerability scanner that first scans a codebase to understand its architecture, then launches targeted AI reviews against high-risk areas to produce vulnerability reports. What stands out is its hybrid architecture: it combines deterministic matching to identify high-risk files with dedicated subagents that inspect them. By narrowing the model's focus to where it matters most, Deepsec can reduce token consumption and cost compared to similar tools.

name: DeepSeek Harness (DSH)
description:
DeepSeek Harness (DSH) is an open-source runtime from DeepSeek AI for building customized coding and general-purpose agents. Rather than offering a monolithic assistant, DSH uses an "everything is a plugin" architecture powered by the Cordis kernel. The model adapter, tool registry, session log and agent loop are all plugins, organized into profiles: named plugin lists that you extend and override in your own YAML.


Cordis is a meta-framework built around spatiotemporal composability: plugins contribute registrations as reversible effects, so reloading and teardown unwind them predictably rather than leaving dangling state. The combination of this plugin architecture and spatiotemporal composability could provide a foundation for domain-specific enterprise harnesses and future self-improving harnesses.


DSH also treats observability as a first-class concern. Every model-visible interaction, including prompts, context injections, tool calls and subagent collaborations, is captured in an append-only session log. This allows runs to be inspected, resumed, forked, searched and replayed, providing a record of what a recomposed system actually did.

name: Entire CLI
description:
Entire CLI hooks into Git to capture coding agent sessions, including prompts, transcripts, tool calls and files touched, and stores them in the repository alongside the commits they produced but outside the branch history. It works with Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, OpenCode, Pi and others. Since we last featured Entire CLI, one of our internal teams that works heavily with coding agents has used it to share every member's sessions. The team found it useful for seeing how teammates prompt, what their agents do with those prompts and how prompting affects the quality of the output. It could also help experienced developers show others how they work with agents.


Openness comes with a cost, however. Entire CLI keeps a permanent record of how each person prompts, and anyone with access to the repository can read it. When we tried introducing it to other teams, some developers pushed back. A coding agent can feel like a personal assistant, and they weren't comfortable sharing everything they asked it with the team. For those teams, AgentsView offers a local alternative, letting developers review their own sessions without sharing them. We suggest trying Entire CLI in highly collaborative teams with a strong culture of trust. It stays in Assess because our experience comes from one internal team, and we don't yet know how other teams can adopt it comfortably.

name: FreeToken
description: FreeToken is an open-source inference engine designed to run large open-weight mixture-of-experts (MoE) models on consumer hardware. As these models become more capable, their full weights can exceed the memory limits of consumer GPUs. Unlike general-purpose local model runners, FreeToken specializes in oversized MoE models by adaptively combining GPU memory, CPU execution, host memory and PCIe bandwidth. It dynamically caches active experts on the GPU and swaps them based on which experts are activated. By coordinating this process, FreeToken enables developers to run much larger models on existing or older hardware. We’re starting to see MoE offloading techniques incorporated into broader tools such as llama.cpp, which is used by Ollama, but FreeToken offers a specialized approach worth assessing.

name: GLM
description:
As the capability gap between open and closed AI models shrinks, the GLM model family by Z.ai stands out for its performance on software engineering workloads. Using a roughly 700-billion-parameter mixture-of-experts (MoE) architecture, models such as GLM-5.3 achieve strong benchmark results in coding, reasoning and agentic tasks, driven largely by specialized post-training rather than pretraining scale alone. This makes GLM-5.3 one of the best open-weight models currently available for coding and software engineering.


We like GLM because it provides teams with an open-weight alternative that competes with proprietary frontier models and complex reasoning tasks. However, in our experience, the model can sometimes "think" too much, overanalyzing straightforward prompts. We advise teams to configure the reasoning effort based on the complexity of the workload.

name: Habit Hooks
description: Habit Hooks is an open-source code-quality coaching tool for AI coding agents. It runs existing static-analysis and linting tools such as Ruff, ESLint, Knip, PMD, deptry and jscpd. Instead of returning raw linter errors, it translates tool-specific rule violations into actionable forward guidance and code smell context. A bare linter violation tells an AI agent that a check has failed but might encourage a superficial change that merely satisfies the rule. Habit Hooks maps the finding to the associated code smell and deterministically injects explicit guidance into the model's prompt. This context helps the agent address the actual design problem and self-correct immediately without relying on an LLM to generate the recommendation. The tool provides a practical implementation of feedback sensors for coding agents, integrating deterministic checks into the implementation loop so agents can respond to failures before human review.

name: Herdr
description:
Herdr is an open-source terminal multiplexer and runtime designed to manage multiple coding agent sessions. It provides familiar multiplexer capabilities such as panes, keyboard navigation, detaching and reattaching, making it easier for developers to migrate from tools such as tmux. Herdr keeps agents running in persistent terminal sessions while exposing agent-aware states such as working, blocked, done and idle. Integrations via a CLI allow agents to create panes, exchange prompts and coordinate work.


As developers increasingly run parallel coding agents across multiple workspaces, keeping track of which sessions require attention and how to resume interrupted work has become a new workflow challenge. Tools such as T3 Code, Orca and Paseo provide alternative experiences for developers who prefer a GUI. Teams managing parallel agents should assess Herdr if they want persistent sessions and visible agent status in their terminal workflow.

name: Hunk
description:
Hunk is an open-source terminal diff viewer for reviewing changes made by coding agents. It displays a GitHub pull request or a Git, Jujutsu or Sapling changeset as a multi-file review with a file sidebar and split or unified layouts. A watch mode refreshes the view as an agent edits the working tree. An agent can load Hunk's agent skill to drive a live review session, jumping to a file or Hunk and adding notes alongside the lines it changed. Reviewers can then read the agent's reasoning next to the relevant code. Those notes distinguish Hunk from syntax-aware diff tools such as Difftastic.


We aren't sure line-by-line human review of agent output will remain the norm, but many teams still need it today: skimping on it can lead to complacency with AI-generated code. The project started in March 2026 and hasn't yet reached version 1.0. Teams that review agent changes in the terminal should try Hunk and assess whether the agent's notes make reviews faster or simply give reviewers more to read.

name: nono.sh
description:
nono.sh is an open-source security shell and lightweight sandbox designed to run AI agents without the overhead of traditional virtual machines or Docker containers. It addresses a common gap: although sandboxing is widely recommended, setup overhead can discourage teams from implementing it. nono.sh isolates agent processes directly at the OS level using native kernel features such as Landlock on Linux and Seatbelt on macOS. It operates in-process as native host processes without background daemons, blocking access to sensitive host assets, such as SSH keys, by default.


We think nono.sh is worth assessing because it lowers the barrier to process isolation. Its minimal design makes it straightforward to configure, test and integrate into existing workflows across macOS, Linux and Windows through WSL2. Security profiles can be tweaked, forked and shared across teams or the broader community through the nono registry, providing a low-overhead layer of defense for developers adopting autonomous tools such as Claude Code or OpenAI Codex.

name: OpenResearch CLI (orx)
description:
OpenResearch CLI (orx) is an open-source harness that turns coding agents such as Claude Code into research agents that run experiments in parallel. Each experiment is isolated in its own Git worktree, so attempts don't interfere with one another. All experiments use the same run command, which keeps results comparable, and every run is pinned to an immutable snapshot of the code for reproducibility.


Because orx runs on compute you choose (local, Slurm, Kubernetes or Modal) teams can implement a method from a paper, reproduce its experiments and then test whether its results hold in their enterprise context. This can help identify the gap between academic results and enterprise practice. We think orx is worth assessing as a promising domain-specific harness for narrowing that gap.

name: Safe Chain
description:
Safe Chain is a free tool from Aikido that wraps the package managers for Node.js and Python, such as npm, pnpm, Bun, pip and uv. It sends package downloads through a local proxy that blocks versions published in the last 48 hours and any package Aikido's open threat feed lists as malicious. Worms such as Shai-Hulud have shown how quickly a compromised package can spread, and a short delay gives scanners time to catch a bad release. Most package managers now have a minimum release age setting, and teams should configure it in their projects. Safe Chain covers what those settings miss, such as a one-off npx command outside any project, or malicious packages older than the age limit.


Safe Chain covers only two ecosystems, but both have been targets of supply chain attacks. A version blocked for its age produces only a generic notice that packages were suppressed. Teams pulling through a private mirror with its own age limit gain little, and the malware blocking depends on a single vendor's feed. Safe Chain is licensed under the AGPL or a commercial license, so check the terms before building it into anything you distribute.

name: Swamp
description:
Swamp is an automation tool built to be used by AI coding agents. When an agent carries out an operational task directly, it may do it differently each time and leave little record of what it did. With Swamp, the agent writes the automation instead, as TypeScript models of external systems and YAML workflows that chain the models' methods together. The workflows follow the same defined process every time, their definitions live in a Git repository and the output from each run is kept as versioned data the agent can query later. Credentials are injected from a vault at runtime, so they stay out of prompts. Models can also be packaged as extensions and shared through a registry. An agent instructed to write and commit scripts without Swamp can produce something similar, but without built-in typed interfaces, run history or reusable modules.


Swamp replaces System Initiative, which we featured in Assess in a previous volume. Swamp grew out of infrastructure management but is aimed at operational workflows more broadly, from incident response to data pipelines. The source is open under AGPLv3, although the official distribution uses a commercial license that requires a subscription for use at work. The project is new and moves fast, with a fresh release for every commit, so teams should try it on low-risk internal automation before depending on it.

name: Vale
description:
Vale is a linter for prose. It parses Markdown, AsciiDoc and reStructuredText, skips code blocks and checks the text against style rules stored as YAML in the repository, so writing conventions can be enforced in the editor and in CI, much like code style. Packaged styles cover the Google, Microsoft and Red Hat documentation guides; others check for inclusive language or readability, and you can write your own. Vale has been part of docs-as-code toolchains for years, but the volume of LLM-drafted documentation, ADRs and PR descriptions makes it more relevant now. Packages such as vail-ai-tells flag the phrasing typical of generated text, and Vale works well as one of the feedback sensors for coding agents, allowing an agent to revise a draft before anyone reads it.


Vale's checks are deterministic word and pattern matches, which can catch surface-level habits but miss weak reasoning or invented detail. Vale also depends largely on one maintainer, and our use so far has been by individuals working on their own writing rather than by client teams.

name: Varlock
description: Varlock is an open-source environment configuration and secrets-management layer designed to avoid exposing secrets to coding agents via plaintext. Instead of relying on informal .env.example conventions, Varlock introduces a committed .env.schema that describes variable names, types, validation rules and documentation. It separates the configuration contract from the actual values. Secrets are resolved and injected at runtime from external vaults such as 1Password, AWS Secrets Manager or Azure Key Vault. For workloads where an agent must call an authenticated service, Varlock also offers a credential proxy that provides a placeholder to the agent and substitutes the real value only at the network boundary. We've found this to be a useful pattern that replaces ad hoc helper scripts and extends secret injection across multiple environments without exposing credentials.

name: zizmor
description:
zizmor is a static analysis tool for GitHub Actions workflows that also checks Dependabot and pre-commit configurations. It flags misconfigurations attackers can exploit, including template injection, overly broad permissions and actions pinned to mutable tags as well as the use of risky triggers such as pull_request_target. It can also fix some findings automatically.


This year, attackers [exploited a pull_request_targetworkflow in the Trivy repository, then rewrote the tags of its GitHub Action so pipelines referencing those tags ran the attackers' code. Our teams have used zizmor on client work, running it from the command line and as a pre-commit hook while writing workflows. Coding agents can run it too, providing quick feedback on the pipelines they write.


Amid the attention on AI-powered security scanning, we like having a deterministic tool for this job. Snyk and Wiz cover some of the same ground commercially and general linters catch some of these issues, but zizmor is free and open source. Its drawback is scope: it doesn’t cover any other CI platforms beyond GitHub Actions. Teams using GitHub Actions should evaluate zizmor alongside zero trust security for CI/CD.
relatedBlips: Zero trust security for CI/CD;GitHub Actions;Wiz;Snyk;Dependabot;Trivy;GitHub

name: Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS)
description:
The Open Data Contract Standard (ODCS) defines data contracts declaratively in YAML, covering a data product's schema, quality expectations and service levels. It’s developed by the Linux Foundation's Bitol project, which graduated in July 2026. Although several competing standards and homegrown formats exist, ODCS has emerged as a leading standard, with the maintainers of Data Contract CLI deprecating DCS in favor of ODCS.


Several of our clients building data meshes and data products are moving to ODCS, often alongside the Open Data Product Standard (ODPS). Interest in data contracts is also growing, partly because their declarative format makes them easier for both humans and AI agents to interpret, review and validate. We’re placing ODCS in Adopt as a sensible default for teams building data products.

name: BoTorch
description:
BoTorch is an open-source, PyTorch-based framework for Bayesian optimization. While Bayesian optimization is often used for hyperparameter tuning, we’re seeing it increasingly applied to real-world scientific and engineering problems. When standard tools for this challenge fall short, BoTorch provides the modularity and low-level control needed to construct probabilistic models and custom acquisition functions.


Paired with Ax for experiment orchestration, BoTorch excels in domains such as product formulation and R&D optimization, where physical or experimental evaluations are costly and exhaustive search is impractical. In these complex search spaces, BoTorch helps teams efficiently navigate trade-offs and maximize a limited evaluation budget.

name: Deep Agents
description:
Deep Agents is an open-source agent harness from LangChain, built for long-running tasks. Deep Agents provides an opinionated architecture for breaking down problems, delegating work to subagents and managing execution. It includes key harness features such as planning tools, agent skills, memory, human-in-the-loop checkpoints and filesystem access.


Available as Python and TypeScript libraries, Deep Agents integrates well with LangChain and LangGraph. It’s particularly useful when specific steps in a complex agentic graph require a capable, long-running agent. In our experience, it complements multi-agent research and legacy modernization use cases and integrates with the broader LangChain ecosystem, including observability tools like Langfuse.

name: Kagent
description:
Kagent is an open-source programming framework and Kubernetes-native platform for building, running and managing AI agents. Instead of requiring bespoke infrastructure, the framework turns agents into standard Kubernetes custom resource definitions (CRDs) that teams can deploy, scale and secure using their existing GitOps pipelines. This allows teams proficient in Kubernetes to build custom agents without needing to learn a new operational model. Kagent provides a built-in runtime with OpenTelemetry, secure sandboxing, memory support and native Model Context Protocol (MCP) integrations to easily connect agents with external tools and model providers.


We've moved Kagent into Trial after successfully using it to support production environments. At a recent client, we transitioned a multi-agent support bot to Kagent from a previous tool that restricted connections to a single MCP server and required hosting on a personal account. Because the client's team was already familiar with Kubernetes, the migration was simple. The resulting deployment features an orchestrator and multiple specialist agents that use Kagent's built-in Agent-to-Agent (A2A) Protocol to communicate, helping developers debug incidents and solve general questions directly within team channels.

name: OpenFGA
description:
⁠OpenFGA is an open-source, fine-grained authorization system inspired by Google’s Zanzibar. It models relationships between users and resources to determine permissions, enabling applications to answer questions such as “Can this user access this resource?”


Unlike traditional role-based access control (RBAC), OpenFGA supports complex, resource-specific permissions and hierarchical relationships. It centralizes authorization logic, improving maintainability, consistency, testing and auditing across distributed services.


We’ve successfully used OpenFGA in production for sophisticated relationship-based access control (ReBAC), deploying it with a sidecar strategy to enable low-latency permission checks. It’s a compelling choice when standard RBAC becomes insufficient.

name: Presidio
description: Presidio is a data protection SDK for identifying and anonymizing sensitive data in structured and unstructured text. It detects personally identifiable information (PII) such as credit card numbers, names and locations using named entity recognition, regular expressions and rule-based logic. Presidio supports custom entity recognizers and de-identification pipelines, allowing organizations to tailor it to their privacy and compliance needs. Our teams have used Presidio in enterprise environments with strict data-sharing controls when integrating with LLMs. While it automates the detection of sensitive information, it isn’t foolproof and may miss or misidentify entities. Teams should exercise caution when relying on its results.

name: Promptfoo
description:
We put Promptfoo in Assess in 2023 for testing prompts. We still use it for evals, including agent tool calls and CI gates, but now also for red teaming. We recommend trialing it for both. To red-team an app, you describe what it's for, and Promptfoo generates attacks for the risks you choose, applies attack strategies and grades the responses.


We used Promptfoo to red-team a production conversational assistant with domain-specific safety rules. It turned ad hoc manual probing into repeatable tests rerun after every fix. It also works with stateful guardrails: the guardrails are the runtime control, and Promptfoo tests that they hold. Promptfoo is now owned by OpenAI, although it remains MIT-licensed and is model agnostic. Some of Promptfoo's more advanced simulated attacks rely on its hosted service, so make sure you're comfortable with what data leaves your organization.

name: Apple Core AI
description:
Apple Core AI is a recently launched framework for running AI and machine-learning models directly on devices using Apple Silicon. Providing native Swift support for mobile development, it acts as the modern successor to Apple's previous framework, Core ML. Apple Core AI allows developers to integrate AI features natively into their iOS applications, using on-device compute rather than relying on external services.


A particularly notable capability in this ecosystem is the Evaluations framework in Xcode, which extends Swift Testing to evaluate generative AI features built with Apple's Foundation Models. Evaluating nondeterministic LLM output has historically required custom back-end scripts or third-party AI evaluation tools. Now, teams can run synthetic datasets, measure quantitative metrics in code and apply model-as-a-judge scoring for qualitative criteria such as tone and relevance, all within native developer workflows.

name: CALM
description:
The Common Architecture Language Model, or ⁠**CALM**, is an open-source specification from FINOS for defining software architectures in a standardized, machine-readable format. Built on an extensible JSON meta-schema, it treats architecture as code rather than relying on static diagrams and documentation that can drift from implementation.


In large enterprises, ensuring systems follow established design patterns can be challenging. CALM allows teams to define and manage architecture in a decentralized way while maintaining a unified view when needed. Its structured descriptions can also support validation against the intended architecture. While tools like Mermaid support diagrams as code, CALM provides a machine-readable foundation for architectural compliance and programmatic governance.

name: Hindsight
description:
Hindsight is Vectorize's open-source memory system for AI agents. An LLM extracts facts, entities and timestamps from conversations and stores them in Postgres. Recall combines semantic, keyword, graph and time-based search and reranks the results. A reflect operation consolidates stored memories into observations and "mental models" that evolve as new evidence arrives. This consolidation sets it apart from Mem0, which extracts and stores the facts it judges most relevant. Hindsight maintains a separate memory bank for each user or agent and can be self-hosted or used through the managed Hindsight Cloud service. Agents connect to it through SDKs, framework integrations or an MCP server.


Hindsight is particularly useful for custom-built agents that need memory across sessions. One of our teams used it in a hackathon project to give agents per-user memory that improves over repeated sessions. Hindsight also has plugins for coding agents such as Claude Code, although those agents already have their own mechanism for retaining memory across sessions. The vendor reports leading scores on the LongMemEval benchmark, which tests recall over long chat histories. Teams building agents that need long-term memory for each user should compare Hindsight with Mem0 and measure whether its recall and consolidation capabilities improve agent behavior enough to justify the additional LLM calls and infrastructure.

name: Quint
description: Quint is a formal specification language based on the underlying calculus of TLA+, the temporal logic of actions. Like TLA+, it's designed to help you find subtle bugs in complex systems involving concurrency. Quint distinguishes itself from TLA+ through its readability and developer experience. It has a TypeScript-like syntax that makes review easier, especially when agents write the specification. It also has a type checker, REPL and simulator and can be installed with npm. The simulator exercises the model inexpensively with randomized runs and can also generate traces from the spec to test an implementation. Our teams have found the choice between Quint and TLA+ a close call, weighing Quint's tooling against TLA+'s maturity. We hope that its ongoing development signals growing momentum behind polyglot verification.

name: SolidJS
description: SolidJS is a declarative JavaScript library for creating user interfaces that continues to stand out for its high performance and fine-grained reactivity. Recent updates introduce significant built-in capabilities for asynchronous client-to-server communication. By handling these concerns natively, SolidJS eliminates the need for external libraries to manage API calls, caching and request deduplication. These features improve the developer experience by addressing common asynchronous challenges, such as race conditions and loading states, directly within the framework. SolidJS also provides detailed control over suspense boundaries, allowing developers to sequence how asynchronous components are revealed rather than leaving their order to network availability. Coupled with an expanding toolset that includes the SolidStart framework, SolidJS is a compelling alternative worth exploring for building high-performance web applications.

name: spartan/ui
description:
spartan/ui applies the approach of shadcn to Angular. You install accessible, unstyled primitives built on the Angular CDK from npm and combine them with styled components that live in your own source code. This division is central to the design: accessibility, behavior and state are maintained by upstream libraries, while you control the styling.


It's a credible Angular Material alternative. One of our teams used it as the basis for a branded component library across several applications, avoiding the need to build a design system from scratch and reducing the effort required to build and maintain shared components. spartan/ui reached version 1.0 in June 2026, but it's still relatively young. We've encountered some rough edges when using the CLI to upgrade the styled components in our source code, so we’re keeping it in Assess.

name: TLA+
description:
TLA+ is a formal specification language for identifying design flaws in distributed systems. When we last blipped it in 2015, the investment was too high for all but critical systems. Since then, coding agents have changed the calculus: the cost of using TLA+ has gone down, while its value has gone up. TLA+'s awkward developer experience is no longer a blocker, although teams looking for friendly syntax might prefer Quint. We've observed teams verify application traces against a TLA+ model without prior experience.


Meanwhile, developers now have greater need for quality assurance techniques to manage agent-generated code. Where TLA+ was once the preserve of organizations like AWS, which used it to find subtle bugs in DynamoDB, it's now part of a broader trend of polyglot verification, alongside techniques like mutation testing and property-based unit testing.
